title: Living Groups and Eyes
audience: Readers who already understand liberties, capture, territory, and ko.
learningGoal: Explain why connection and eye shape determine whether a group lives or dies.

steps.title: Two separate eyes
steps.text: Black's corner group is surrounded by White, but it has two separate internal {{liberty:liberties}} at A1 and C1. Each is an {{eye}}: White cannot legally fill either point without self-capture. A group with two secure eyes lives.

steps.title: Shape, not stone count
steps.text: Raw stone count is not enough. A surrounded group can still live when its shape gives it protected internal liberties. Survival depends less on having many stones than on building a form the opponent cannot legally or efficiently eliminate.

steps.title: Connection
steps.text: A {{connection}} turns separate stones into one unit. Connected stones share liberties, answer attacks together, and can build internal shape more efficiently than isolated stones. Local fights are often fights over cutting and connecting.

steps.title: Eyes and life
steps.text: An {{eye}} is a protected empty point inside a group's shape. A group with two secure eyes normally lives; a group that cannot make two eyes may die. Life-and-death reading asks whether a group can form those eyes before its opponent seals it in.

steps.title: Why local shape matters
steps.text: Life-and-death judgment changes whole-board strategy. Saving a living group can preserve a large territorial framework; killing an invading group can turn a contested region into secure {{territory}}.

steps.title: Exercise 1
steps.prompt: Why is a connected group usually stronger than the same stones scattered apart?
steps.answer: Connected stones share {{liberty:liberties}}, defend each other, and can build eyes as one unit. Scattered stones can be cut apart and attacked separately.

steps.title: Exercise 2
steps.prompt: Why does the phrase "two eyes live" matter more than raw stone count?
steps.answer: A group survives by preserving secure internal liberties, not by merely having many stones. Two proper eyes usually make capture impossible under ordinary play.

steps.title: What comes next
steps.text: Use the new vocabulary in a tsumego problem, or return to the first lesson's worked example.
